Experiments span diverse settings: a 1,200-snapshot synthetic problem, 115-frame cell tracking, 5–100 dimensional scRNA-seq, and spatial transcriptomics, with comparisons to recent CFM, MFM, and MMFM methods.

weaknesses: Theorem 2.2 is invalid as stated. Its proof constructs G(x0,x1,t) as a function of the reference interpolant, which additionally depends on x_ti, although G is restricted to inputs (x0,x1,t). Absolute continuity of the reference distribution does not resolve this measurability and feasibility problem, and existence or uniqueness can fail. This directly undermines the prominently claimed uniqueness guarantee.

More broadly, both uniqueness results concern exact, population-level marginal constraints independently at each fixed time. The implemented finite-weight, finite-sample GAN objective neither enforces these constraints exactly nor inherits uniqueness, and pointwise uniqueness does not establish a smooth or unique trajectory across time. Thus the theory does not substantiate the paper's claims about the actual learned interpolants.

The two experiments intended to demonstrate the method's clearest advantages are evaluated almost entirely through selected visualizations. The synthetic experiment has known distributions, and the cell-tracking experiment has full segmentation masks, yet neither reports quantitative marginal or trajectory errors, multiple seeds, uncertainty, or a systematic diagnosis of baseline divergence.

ALI-CFM is consistently worse than OT-MFM in every reported scRNA-seq setting across Tables 1 and 2, including all high-dimensional cases, and is sometimes worse than OT-CFM. Consequently, these results provide little support for superior performance or scalability; no runtime or memory measurements are given either.

The spatial-transcriptomics headline result is based on one specimen and only two possible held-out sections, with no clear number of runs or significance test. Moreover, preprocessing manually aligns every section using its H&E image—including the held-out section—and chooses the tumor threshold by visual agreement, making the test-time information and potential leakage unclear. Alignment uncertainty and cross-patient generalization are not evaluated.

There are no ablations isolating the adversarial loss, the three proposed regularizers, endpoint coupling, pretraining, time noise, or regularization strength. Substantially different recipes are used across datasets, including a different GAN objective and a LAND-modified regularizer, so it is unclear which component produces the reported behavior.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness are insufficient for a complex adversarial method. No code is provided, and important details are missing or ambiguous, including min-max update signs and scheduling, the precise R3GAN loss, finite-difference step and boundary handling, OT construction and regularization, EMD computation, ODE tolerances, and several seed counts. MMFM is modified, multi-marginal MFM is omitted in one key experiment, and training budgets and model capacities differ across methods.

The claimed continuous-time applicability is not evaluated, and positioning against broader snapshot-dynamics and trajectory-inference approaches is limited. Overall, the appealing idea is not supported by sufficiently sound theory or sufficiently controlled empirical evidence for acceptance.

GAN matching is imposed only at observed discrete times and is approximate, while the stated results assume exact marginal constraints. In particular, the linear regularizer evaluated at those times does not uniquely determine the curve between observations. Missing finite-moment and regularity assumptions further weaken the formal statements.

The empirical support for the strongest claims is limited. The knot experiment and the single-cell-tracking experiment are primarily qualitative; the latter uses one cell from one sequence and explicitly omits quantitative evaluation. Divergence of selected baseline runs does not establish an inherent limitation without controlled solver, optimization, and hyperparameter studies.

On scRNA-seq, OT-MFM is better than OT-ALI-CFM in every one of the seven reported settings, often by considerably more than the reported run-to-run variation. Thus the claim of state-of-the-art-level performance or compelling high-dimensional scalability is not supported by the main quantitative benchmark.

The spatial-transcriptomics result uses one specimen with four manually aligned sections and only two possible held-out sections. The paper does not clearly define what Table 3 averages over or provide per-section results, statistical tests, or sensitivity to manual landmarks, the visually selected tumor threshold, and access to held-out-section images during alignment.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness remain inadequate: no implementation is provided; the main text specifies a classical GAN objective while the single-cell experiments use R3GAN; the regularizer weight is adjusted through an unspecified value-matching procedure; validation/model-selection protocols are unclear; and training cost is not compared despite a two-stage 70,000-step adversarial procedure.
